pages.title: I'm from… / She's from…
rules: Use from + country or city to say where you come from.
In English the verb be is always needed: I'm from…, not I from…
Countries start with a capital letter.

pages.title: The sound /θ/ and /ð/
pages.tip: Put the tongue between your teeth and blow: thhhree. In Portuguese we do not have this sound! It appears in three, thanks, Thursday, and in 'the' (voiced /ð/).

pages.head: Neighbors from far away
text: Maple Street is a small street with big dreams. Mia is from Brazil. She is a teacher. Ken is from Japan and he is a chef. Sara is from Egypt. She is a nurse. Tom is from England and he is a driver.
They speak different languages. Mia speaks Portuguese, Ken speaks Japanese, Sara speaks Arabic and Tom speaks English. But in the street, everybody speaks English together.
Every Friday there is a street party. People bring food from their countries. There is feijoada from Brazil, sushi from Japan, koshari from Egypt and fish and chips from England!
tf: Everybody speaks English in the street.
There is a street party every Friday.
pages.talk: What food from your country would you bring to the party?

pages.title: Countries: fact file

facts.label: English speakers by country
facts.sub: the USA has the most native speakers

text: English is the first language in countries like the USA, the UK, Australia and Canada. It is also an official language in India, Nigeria and South Africa.
People from the UK are British. People from England are English. People from the USA are American.
When someone asks 'Where are you from?', you can say your country or your city.
